beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on the last question in this series: why the team hasn't fine-tuned an A.I. model for physics yet. It's the exciting option. Train a model on physics, and make it smarter. But the team wrote down exactly when they'd do it, and that trigger hasn't fired.

props.command: Why hasn't the physics engine team fine-tuned a model for physics yet?
output: Fine-tuning waits on a written trigger
The engine isn't wrong; it's thin
More formula cards, not a smarter model

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, how the team knows the engine is right: the golden set. Second, what an outside benchmark actually says. And third, the rule for when fine-tuning makes sense, and why it hasn't fired. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. The project plan makes fine-tuning conditional: only if results plateau below target, with full coverage of the formula library. Neither is true. The engine isn't getting answers wrong. It's declining problems it has no card for. More cards would fix that. A smarter model wouldn't.

First, how they know it's right. The golden set is sixteen problems across mechanics, and electricity and magnetism, each with a checked answer. The engine matches all sixteen. One was also checked against a published textbook. OpenStax gives three point two seven meters per second squared. The engine gives three point two six six seven. The same answer, rounded.

Then the outside test: UGPhysics, one thousand two hundred twenty-six undergraduate problems. Only eighteen percent can score the engine as it stands, because most of the rest ask for a derivation, a formula, not a number. Topic coverage looks like seventy-nine percent. But the team calls that a ceiling. One card can touch a topic without covering it.

On sixty of those problems: zero wrong answers, and nearly everything declined. Nothing plateaued. In the team's words, there's no evidence a better model would help, and considerable evidence that more formula cards would. The bottleneck is coverage, not intelligence.

So starting fine-tuning now would be, in their words, exactly the kind of decision the decision log exists to prevent: doing the interesting work instead of the indicated work. It's the same reason quantum physics was left out. Weak quantum cards would make the coverage number go up, while the thing the engine is for got worse. And if a fine-tuned model ever comes, the golden set decides. It ships only when it beats the benchmark, never on hope.

What's still open, from their own status table. The golden set is far short of the hundred fifty to three hundred problems first planned. The baseline, plain A.I. reasoning on the same problems, has never been run, and that's the number the whole project is justified by. And nothing is deployed yet.

So here's the takeaway, for the whole series. Before you reach for a bigger model, find out what's actually failing. Measure first. Then build what the measurement points at, even when it's the boring thing.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude about any project you're working on. It asks Claude to find the real bottleneck before suggesting a fix.

props.command: Here is my project and what's going wrong: [describe it]. Before suggesting any fix, list what has actually been measured, what hasn't, and where the failures really come from. Then recommend the one change the evidence points to, even if it's the boring one.
output: Where the failures really come from
The one change the evidence points to
